On May 5 last year, Hartford High hooper Charlotte Jasmin underwent surgery on a torn ACL. One year later to the day, the senior shared a full-circle moment with those closest to her at her signing day, where she declared her intent to play for the University of New Hampshire in the fall. Jasmin averaged 25.5 points, 10 rebounds, 6.1 steals, and 4.7 assists this past season, was named the Gatorade Player of the Year for the second time, eclipsed 2,000 career points, and helped lead her squad to a VPA Division II state title. “I got to sign to play Division I basketball on the same day that I was starting recovery, so that was kind of crazy,” the 5-foot-10 guard said. “It was fantastic to have that in my home court gym one last time, where I got to sit there and have a moment and have all the people that have been around for everything around me.” In addition to fulfilling a dream of playing Division I basketball in the America East Conference, Jasmin also emphasized how she connected with the Wildcats’ head coach and players. title: UNH project for major research and mixed-use community underway in Durham - New Hampshire Public Radio
content:
This story was originally produced by the Portsmouth Herald. NHPR is republishing it in partnership with the Granite State News Collaborative. University of New Hampshire officials expect the state economy will be bolstered with the development of The Edge, a massive mixed-use, research and residential community planned for the western portion of the school’s campus. In November, UNH and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration broke ground on the new 70,500-square-foot Center of Excellence for Operational Ocean and Great Lakes Mapping, The Edge’s crown jewel. Marc Eichenberger, the university’s vice president and chief business development and innovation officer, and Jennifer Miksis-Olds, the school’s interim vice president for research and innovation, reported the center should be operational and welcoming in students, faculty, scientists and industry business partners by November 2027. The cost of building the Center of Excellence for Operational Ocean and Great Lakes Mapping alone is projected to cost $34 million, said Eichenberger. The majority of the project is federally funded, with $20 million contributed by NOAA and another $5 million from the National Institute for Standards and Technology. title: UNH Stock Moves Higher as UnitedHealth Cuts Prior Approval Rules and CVS Adds Cost Signal - TechStock²
content: UnitedHealth Group shares climbed Wednesday, catching fresh attention as the company’s insurance business announced it’s dropping prior authorization on a wide range of procedures that still required it. UNH last traded at $367.55, up roughly 1% for the session. The stock moved between $358.24 and $368.50 intraday. Timing is key here. Prior authorization—when insurers sign off before patients can get certain treatments—has turned into a battleground not just for doctors and patients, but also for policymakers. Investors are paying close attention to whether managed-care firms can ease these headaches without losing grip on cost controls. On Tuesday, Reuters said UnitedHealth plans to drop prior approval for 30% of medical services that still require it. UnitedHealthcare plans to roll out the cuts by the end of 2026, targeting select outpatient surgeries, some diagnostic tests—including echocardiograms—and certain outpatient therapies along with chiropractic care. According to the company, just 2% of its medical services now need prior authorization, and roughly 92% of those requests get the green light in under 24 hours on average. UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel called prior authorization “an essential safeguard,” though he added it “should only be used when it truly protects patients and improves care.” The company said it expects over 70% of its prior authorizations to move to a standardized electronic submission process by the end of the year. The shift comes as the broader industry makes a similar push. Back in April, UnitedHealth and CVS Health announced they’d lined up data and submission requirements for over half their prior authorizations. CVS’s Aetna reported 88% of its authorizations were standardized at that point. UnitedHealthcare emphasized that the updates wouldn’t affect coverage criteria or the medical standards for approving or rejecting care. UnitedHealth isn’t dealing with the prior-approval cut in isolation. Just last month, the company posted first-quarter revenue of $111.7 billion, with adjusted earnings landing at $7.23 per share. The full-year adjusted profit outlook climbed above $18.25 a share. Medical cost ratio dropped to 83.9%, down from 84.8% in the same period last year. Analysts saw the report as an early signal of a turnaround for health insurers after a rough patch. Ann Hynes of Mizuho described it as a “positive quarter,” noting that medical cost acceleration seemed to have topped out. Michael Wiederhorn at Oppenheimer, on his end, said UnitedHealth appeared ready to get back to its “beat-and-raise ways.” Reuters Rival headlines set the tone for trading. CVS jumped over 9% after the company boosted its 2026 profit outlook Wednesday, crediting tighter Aetna medical cost controls and a stronger pharmacy-benefit showing. The Aetna medical loss ratio landed at 84.6%, beating analyst forecasts. UnitedHealth and Humana, on the other hand, have both flagged continued pressure from Medicare Advantage costs. There’s risk here. Streamlining approval steps might placate frustrated doctors and patients, but it could open the door to scrutiny over utilization if more services slip past with lighter review. UnitedHealth’s first-quarter materials flagged that both utilization and unit-cost trends stayed high, despite the company touting improved medical cost controls. For UNH stock, it’s not Tuesday’s news that matters most, but how things play out from here. Eyes are on the second-quarter medical cost ratio, the definitive lineup of services dropping prior approval, and whether Medicare Advantage—covering seniors and some disabled Americans—continues the more solid trend seen earlier this year. title: What Can You Do With an MPA? - University of New Hampshire
content: Balancing midnight police shifts with evening graduate courses, Kathryn Mone proved that Carsey's Master's of Public Administration (MPA) program is designed for working professionals ready to lead. But what is an MPA good for? What jobs can you get with the degree? The public administration field has a seat in every industry, from health care and education to government, law enforcement, and every major sector in between. The MPA program focuses on designing, implementing, and evaluating policies and services in any organization, giving Kathryn the perfect foundation for a leadership role in local government and law enforcement. My experience with the MPA program, we learned how local government works, that law enforcement is just a piece of local government...so I'm glad I have that wider view." That "wider view" has taken her farther than most women in law enforcement. In 2024, Kathryn became Strafford County's first female elected sheriff, a distinction shared by fewer than 2% of sheriffs nationwide. When making the decision to earn her master's degree, Kathryn didn't have the luxury of stepping away from her career to go back to school full-time. Working at the Durham, New Hampshire, Police Department with aspirations of stepping into an administrative leadership role, she needed a program that would give her the credentials to elevate her career while being flexible to her life outside the program. Carsey's MPA did just that. Night classes made the school-work-life balance possible, allowing Kathryn to attend lectures before heading to her shift at the police station. Now 100% online, the MPA continues to be tailored for mid-career professionals who want to grow without pressing the pause button on their lives. In law enforcement, it's easy to only focus on the goals of the department—reducing crime, community needs, staffing, etc. But Kathryn's MPA studies broadened her perspective beyond the scope of the department. She came to understand how every department—fire, planning, city management—all work together to support the community. That full-scope view made her a stronger leader, helping her to see law enforcement as one piece of the much larger system. That perspective helps her to reach her personal mission of reshaping how communities view law enforcement by building trust and approachability. When I started, I wanted to change what people thought of as a typical law enforcement officer...If you need to talk to a law enforcement officer about anything that's happened, I want you to think, I can call Kathryn. And when that happens, when I get those calls, I know my career has been worth it. Kathryn's coursework wasn't just theory; it was applied projects taught by practitioners in the field that connected directly to her career. I had one professor who worked for public sector unions...And I, at the time, was in the union as a police officer. And now I president of the union. And I think it was such a good basis. Before I really knew anything about unions, I learned it in class from someone who was working in the field. As a part of her journey, Kathryn got the opportunity to go out in the field for tangible project experience. Traveling to the western side of New Hampshire, her cohort worked alongside a small town council to help them with a community-facing project. This wasn't only a service to the town but also proved to be valuable to Kathryn's career. During her time serving as North Hampton's chief of police, she helped gain community support for new police and fire facilities. It was in this process that she drew directly from what she learned in the program about bonds, bids, and local government. The passing of the construction project was a wonderful example of how local government works and how New Hampshire government works. A distinguished leader in her field, Kathryn is doing her part to give back to her law enforcement community. Growing up with the itch to teach, the MPA program has given her both the credentials and the confidence to do just that. In addition to her duties as Sheriff, she also teaches criminal justice classes at Great Bay Community College. Now she's not only using lessons from her program to build trust and relationships in the community, but also to instill it in the next generation of leaders in the field—developing the approachable law enforcement members she once wished for. It's definitely worth it. I think wherever you are, Iust getting out of school or [having] been in the workforce a while, the Public Administration Master's is very valuable. Kathryn's journey is one example of how an MPA can open doors beyond a single career track. No matter the field you're in—law enforcement, education, nonprofit management—the MPA equips graduates with the skills to lead, collaborate, and drive change. For Kathryn, the MPA wasn't just a box to check on her resume; it was a path to leadership in her community and a chance to be the change she wanted to see. A public administration degree is an interdisciplinary program that trains students to examine policy, programs, law, and finances in the context of public-facing organizations and their impact on society. Both the public administration and public policy programs focus on introducing students to global issues with the goal of strategic problem-solving and communication. MPP programs prepare students to analyze, evaluate, and construct policies, while MPA students are trained to plan, lead, and implement those policies. title: First-Year Students Win Holloway Competition with Virtual Reality Gaming Venture - University of New Hampshire
content: Armored Pig Studios team members Dylan Nye, Kinoa Witt and Aidan Cronin pose with the $15,000 grand prize check after winning the 38th Paul J. Holloway Prize Innovation to Market Competition. It’s never too early to move forward with a great idea. A trio of first-year students with a passion for virtual reality gaming proved just that, taking home the $15,000 grand prize at the 38th Paul J. Holloway Prize Innovation to Market Competition. Armored Pig Studios — made up of Kinoa Witt, Dylan Nye and Aidan Cronin — impressed judges with their business plan focused on developing and designing virtual reality games. The team has already found success on the Meta platform with its game Buddy Beatdown, a multiplayer, stress-relief sandbox experience where players can creatively fight a ragdoll character. The group is actively developing additional games as it builds momentum. “I think the numbers set us apart,” Witt says. “What we’re building isn’t just an idea — we’re well past that stage. What really sets us apart is that we have the proof and the data to back it up. We’ve already reached hundreds of thousands of users, which shows that VR is not just interesting — it’s an industry worth pursuing.” Though only in their first year at UNH, the team draws on a range of complementary experiences. Witt, a computer science major, has been involved in virtual reality development for four years; Nye, a liberal arts major, brings experience in game design; and Cronin, a finance major, supports market analysis as the business grows. “This is my fourth year in VR development, so it’s really rewarding to win this competition and have that time validated,” Witt says. “For me, it means more time to keep building. The $15,000 will help with costs and allow us to continue expanding and scaling.” Named in honor of Paul J. Holloway, an accomplished business leader and successful entrepreneur, the Holloway competition is USNH's premier business plan competition for undergraduate and graduate students across the university system. Armored Pig Studios may have taken home the top prize, but the five other finalists also left strong impressions on judges and received awards of their own. In total, 34 teams entered this year’s competition. Other business ideas pitched during the finals included innovations in research collaboration, indoor rock-climbing technology, AI business solutions, government services, and workplace productivity tools. Ethan O’Leary of OmniClimb, a venture developing technology that provides indoor rock climbers with real-time performance feedback, presents during the Holloway Competition. OmniClimb won the Sustainable Impact Award. UNH President Elizabeth Chilton noted that all finalists benefited from the experience, regardless of the outcome. “These are creative ideas that meet real-world needs. But just as important as what students develop is what they learn along the way. We don’t move from an initial idea to a final pitch without refining it, adjusting it or often rethinking it entirely,” Chilton says. “Working through uncertainty, getting feedback and continuing to improve is exactly the kind of iterative process that prepares students — whether it's your first year or you're a graduating doctoral student — for their careers and for life.” Chilton credited the UNH Entrepreneurship Center for helping to build an entrepreneurial ecosystem where students from any major can bring an idea forward, find collaborators, and find support to explore it. Paul College Dean Lucy Gilson says that seeing students from multiple disciplines collaborate highlights the strength of the competition. “This is the cornerstone of what we do. We educate our students both inside and outside of the classroom,” Gilson says. “Experiential learning is important to all of us, and the magic happens when you see students from different colleges come together.” Below are the results of the 2026 Holloway Competition and additional information on the six finalists. Kinoa Witt, ’29, computer science (founder & lead dev) Dylan Nye, ’29, liberal arts (level design & assistant game design) Armored Pig Studios develops and designs virtual reality games. What problem are you solving — and why does it matter? Virtual reality gaming is still in its infancy, and a vast majority of games available are low-quality or simply not enjoyable. We develop engaging, social experiences designed to maximize player enjoyment and retention. Our founder and developer, Kinoa Witt, has been working in the virtual reality space for five years. Last fall, he founded Armored Pig Studios. How did your team come together, and how did your different academic backgrounds contribute to the venture? During welcome week at UNH, we all met each other as freshmen. We all share a love for video games and technology, and Kinoa had already shipped multiple virtual reality games onto the Meta Quest store. Naturally, everyone was interested, and eventually we realized the benefits we could gain from working together. Our biggest challenge is maintaining the active development of multiple titles while being students. We have learned many lessons in prioritization, time management, and all-night sprints. What are your next steps for the venture after Holloway? For our newest game, Buddy Beatdown, we are working with publisher 2080 Games. They funded the development of the game, handled platform listings, distribution, and assisted in game design. We will continue to develop and expand Buddy Beatdown while developing and shipping new titles. Agent Integrator is an AI transformation firm and venture studio that builds vertical AI agents for small and mid-sized businesses and enterprises. The company develops end-to-end systems that automate operations and, when scalable, turns them into products or co-built ventures with industry partners. What problem are you solving — and why does it matter? Many businesses know they need to adopt AI but don’t know how to apply it effectively to their operations. Agent Integrator focuses on identifying operational bottlenecks — like overwhelmed staff, inefficient workflows, and manual processes — and replacing them with AI-driven systems that allow companies to scale without increasing headcount. In one example, a multi-location dermatology practice was handling more than 200 calls a day, with wait times reaching 20 minutes. Agent Integrator is building a 21-agent system to manage inbound calls, scheduling, and operations across locations, reducing strain on staff and improving efficiency. One of the biggest challenges has been scaling the business while managing internal constraints, particularly the audit process required to understand each client’s workflows. Mapping how teams operate, documenting processes, and accounting for edge cases can be complex and time-consuming, directly limiting how many clients the company can take on at once. Another challenge is balancing growth with talent acquisition. Highly skilled engineers are in high demand, so the company has had to develop alternative compensation models — such as revenue-sharing per project — to attract and retain talent. The immediate focus is scaling the business to $2 million in revenue by the end of 2026. To get there, Agent Integrator plans to expand beyond inbound leads by building an outbound sales engine and forming partnerships with go-to-market agencies. The team is also working to remove internal bottlenecks by systemizing the audit process and hiring additional support, allowing multiple client engagements to run in parallel. Longer term, the goal is to transition from a services-heavy model into more scalable products — turning the systems they build into repeatable, software as a service (SaaS)  offerings and co-developed ventures within specific industries. Fatima Hanif, fourth-year Ph.D. student, civil & environmental engineering King-James Egbe, fourth-year Ph.D. student, civil & environmental engineering Nizar Alhalabi, third-year Ph.D. student, civil & environmental engineering Kwasi Owusu-Boateng third-year Ph.D. student, economics Lablincs is an online ecosystem for researchers — a better way for students and advisors to discover relevant work, showcase their contributions, and connect to find the right research fit, whether as trainees, mentors, or collaborators. What problem are you solving and why does it matter? Student–advisor relationships often begin with incomplete information. Students don’t fully understand lab expectations, and advisors can’t assess how a student actually works. These mismatches can cost time, funding, and well-being. The Lablincs online platform improves this by helping both sides make more informed, intentional matches. The idea came from our own experiences as Ph.D. students and conversations with faculty. Both groups expressed frustration with a process that relies heavily on assumptions and incomplete applications. How did your team come together, and how have your different academic backgrounds contributed to the venture? The venture has been shaped by our experiences in research and our exposure to the academic system, and we’ve been actively improving it through conversations across disciplines. In addition to our combined three decades in academia, we bring leadership experience, multicultural perspectives, and exposure to multiple educational systems across continents, along with deep expertise in fields such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, product design, and finance. Each perspective adds a distinct layer, whether it’s understanding how admissions decisions are made, how students evaluate programs, or how mentoring relationships evolve over time. This cross-disciplinary, cross-cultural input is shaping how we think about the platform and ensuring it is not built from a single viewpoint. The biggest challenge has been translating a problem that people feel intuitively into something measurable and actionable. Everyone agrees that “fit” matters, but defining what that means, and how to capture it in a structured way, is not straightforward. It’s been a process of breaking down something very human and nuanced into components that can be evaluated without oversimplifying it. Another challenge has been balancing research and venture development, especially while being in a Ph.D. program. Was there a UNH program, resource, or connection that helped move this idea forward? With an idea like ours, a university is the perfect nursery and test bed, because you can find everything you need to succeed in one place. Departments like the ECenter and opportunities such as the Holloway Competition have pushed us to think more clearly about the problem, validate our assumptions, and communicate the idea more effectively. Faculty mentorship and conversations within the UNH research community have also been incredibly valuable in grounding the idea in real-world experiences. What are your next steps for the venture after Holloway? We’re currently working with faculty and students to test the platform and refine the matching process. At the same time, we’re expanding our network of early adopters and building pilot partnerships within labs and departments. Long term, the goal is to improve match quality, reduce screening time, and scale the platform beyond an initial group of institutions. Climbers access this information on the OmniClimb mobile app to gain insights into their current abilities, habits, and trends. What problem are you solving — and why does it matter? At the same time, it’s one of the fastest-growing sports in the U.S. OmniClimb addresses this gap by providing an accessible, personalized coaching platform — delivering critical feedback to help climbers improve. With more than 15 years of combined climbing experience, we’ve seen how difficult it is to improve without feedback. In a sport defined by gradual progression, limited insight can be demotivating. OmniClimb grew from a simple question: How can we help climbers improve after each session, especially without access to affordable coaching? Ethan and Blaise met through UNH Campus Recreation’s Outdoor Adventures Program, where Ethan managed climbing walls and built community connections. title: Why Get an Accelerated Master's in Justice Studies? - University of New Hampshire
content: The field of justice studies involves philosophical and theoretical understandings of justice, knowledge of the inner-workings and realities of laws and justice systems, and skills related to the implementation of justice. Pursuing a master’s in justice studies allows you to delve deeply into law, crime, courts, corrections, policing, drugs, terrorism, homeland security, immigration, forensics, sexual violence, juvenile justice, and more. Meet Cassidy Barcome '26, who is getting an accelerated master's degree in justice studies at UNH. Along the way, she's found a wealth of research opportunities, an internship in the field of juvenile justice, and a close-knit cohort of peers. Learn more about how you will save time and money with an accelerated graduate degree from UNH. Why did you decide to do a master’s in justice studies at UNH? An important reason I chose to attend UNH for graduate school was because of the possible opportunities I could seize while I am here. UNH is rich in research and opportunities within the juvenile justice field, with two examples being the Crimes Against Children Research Center and the Sibling-on-Sibling Aggression and Abuse Model. It just seemed like the right fit for me given my previous experience and my goals for the future. As a student who was previously unfamiliar with UNH, the faculty have been more than welcoming to me as I entered this program. Professors also make themselves easily available for office hours to give extra support if I need it. What are some of the coolest experiences you’ve had? I have been fortunate enough to intern with Juvenile Probation and Parole of Rochester, New Hampshire. This is a particular role in the juvenile justice field that I am interested in long-term, so this experience has been excellent for me. Additionally, the relationships I’ve created with my cohort have absolutely made this program special for me.  We have become a very close-knit team, which has been an incredible experience to have. "Professors also make themselves easily available for office hours to give extra support if I need it." My internship has been immensely valuable to me and my career goals. In my opinion, gaining hands-on experience in this field is crucial for success. Academic knowledge of the criminal justice system is important; however, gaining experience in this field is vital to ensure you are both in the right role, and equipped to handle the challenging dynamics that will inevitably present themselves. What is your area of interest and why did you choose it? I graduated from Southern New Hampshire University (SNHU) in Manchester, New Hampshire, with a BA in psychology, concentrating in forensics. While at SNHU, I interned with the Child Advocacy Center of Laconia, New Hampshire. After graduating, I then found employment as a children’s case manager and care coordinator before deciding to pursue graduate school. Juvenile justice is my professional passion, which is why UNH seemed like a good fit for me. "In my opinion, gaining hands-on experience in this field is crucial for success." How is your current job complementing what you’re learning in your program? Outside of graduate school, I am employed by Somersworth Police Department (PD) as a dispatcher. Although still new to the role, I am really enjoying my time with Somersworth PD and have learned a lot from them. I have been fortunate enough to experience various roles both in employment and internships that have allowed me to gain a well-rounded view of the justice system. Having these experiences allows me to apply real world knowledge to what I learn in my courses. "I have been fortunate enough to experience various roles both in employment and internships that have allowed me to gain a well-rounded view of the justice system." What are some of the most important skills you’ve gained through your program? Some skills I’ve gained within my time at UNH include strengthening my research and critical thinking skills, as well as advancing in collaboration and project management skills. Why would you recommend this program to a prospective student? I would recommend this program to any student who is looking to gain some more experience before jumping into the working world. I would also recommend this program to any student who enjoys research. What are some of your favorite things to do near UNH? UNH is in a very cool area of New Hampshire with tons of different things to explore and easy access to Maine or Massachusetts. In my free time, I can be found at the Suite Studio, a fitness studio in Dover, New Hampshire! I adore going to class there and being part of their community. Other than that, I love going to Regal Cinemas as much as I can, and spending time with my friends. I also recently started the process of volunteering with the Pope Memorial Humane Society - Cocheco Valley, an animal shelter in Dover. "UNH is in a very cool area of New Hampshire with tons of different things to explore and easy access to Maine or Massachusetts." I still have a bit of time left in my program, which is where my focus is right now. I will be happy to seize opportunities that present themselves to me when the time comes, but I’m thoroughly enjoying where things have taken me so far! title: Extension Helps Convert Historic North Country Farm to Apple Orchard - University of New Hampshire
content: Both products of Northeastern apple valleys – he’s from Concord and she’s from Binghamton, New York – Doug Morin and Emily Meacham wanted the home they would make for themselves to be on an apple orchard. One problem: they were looking for something in the northern half of either New Hampshire or Vermont, and there were no established orchards for sale. Instead of a mom-and-pop-sized orchard, they settled on a former beef and dairy farm that was much larger than the parcel they had envisioned. The fact that Tellman Hill Farm in Bethlehm, New Hampshire is now producing fruit from hundreds of trees is a testament to the determination and flexibility of its owners, as well as robust support from UNH Extension. The Extension specialists who help support such ventures say that their work does more than support one family and enhance the local food supply chain; it can serve as a benefit to numerous other businesses in the region. Morin is trained as a wildlife biologist and Meacham is a forester. They met while both were working for the state of Vermont, and one thing they shared in common was a love of New England’s most prolific fruit. “There’s a little bit of childhood nostalgia — apple orchards are neat,” Morin says. Meacham adds that there’s practical benefits as well. “We knew we wanted to be farmers and Doug doesn’t like bending over for vegetables,” she says. “We both have had an interest in apple trees for a long time.” They like the agritourism aspect of pick-your-own operations as well as the flexibility to experiment with other products, such as chickens, decorative gourds, and cut flowers. Their plan was for Meacham to keep her position as a forester, which meant they needed to look for a property within driving distance of her office in northern Vermont. Their dream was a cozy little orchard with established trees. Their reality would require them to build that dream. Located on high ground, as the name suggests, the Tellman Hill Farm was a retired dairy and beef farm when Morin and Meacham found it. Easements on the property meant that it had to be used for agricultural purposes, which was just fine by them. The biggest problem, aside from its lack of apple trees, was its size. Tellman Hill Farm is 60 acres, a larger bite of orchard than they were initially planning to chew. “When we had the opportunity and this property came on our radar, that caused us to scale up our operation,” Morin says. They set out looking for a hobby farm and ended up with a commercial-size property. Meacham and Morin bought the property in 2019. Two other important things happened that year. The first was that they placed their first call to UNH Extension, and soon thereafter walked their property with Heather Bryant, fruit and vegetable production field specialist. “Heather was really the first person we talked through our ideas,” Meacham says. “She was the first person to give us confidence to go forward.” The other important thing was ordering their first batch of trees — 500 of them. An order of that size has to be placed two years in advance, and those trees were planted in 2021, the same year they formed an LLC for their business. So, smooth sailing? Hardly, but they have survived so far, with a little help. The new orchardists, with their combined expertise in wildlife and trees, were unusually well-suited to grow fruit in the woods of northern New Hampshire. Even so, their learning curve was steep, and with the size of their operation — they now have more than 1,000 apple trees — there was no such thing as a small problem. Tellman Hill Farm’s early challenges included drought, wind damage, mole and vole pressure, and learning the nuances of integrated pest management. One particular episode captures what Extension services does for an operation like Tellman Hill. Meacham noticed some strange symptoms in their seedlings during leaf-out one year, and called in Will Hastings, Coos County field specialist, for a look. Hastings referred the case to Bo Liu, director of UNH’s Plant Diagnostics Lab, who confirmed that a fungus was to blame. Next up was Jeremy DeLisle, fruit specialist, who shared how other growers manage the fungus, while Renuka Mathur, soil health specialist for Extension, gave them tips for improving soil health. Thanks to the early diagnosis and intervention, those trees were saved. Had they ignored the initial symptoms, the fungus would likely have killed the young trees, the new orchardists would have had to wait two years for new saplings to be ready, and those replacement trees would likely have also succumbed to the fungus, setting them back two more years. Extension’s expertise, offered free of charge, represents a significant investment into Morin and Meacham’s business. The experts so eagerly offer their expertise because the benefits extend well beyond Tellman Hill. Hastings notes that Extension helped the orchard to secure a federal Regional Food Systems Infrastructure grant to build a commercial kitchen. “This facility could be used by other farms in the region to provide value-added products,” Hastings notes. But that’s only one of the ways the orchard might boost its neighbors. Hastings suggests that official estimates of the impact of orchard-based businesses are undervalued. That belief is supported by a recent study by Cornell University, which measured the benefit of New York State’s apple farms to be $574 million in 2016, 21% higher than the state’s official estimate. The difference was due to the failure of the official studies to consider how those businesses spend their income, not just how much they make. Jeremy DeLisle, fruit production field specialist for Extension, is trying to get a firm handle on how to estimate the economic value of New Hampshire’s apple growers, who sell a range of related products such as cider doughnuts. “You’d be surprised how many doughnuts some of these apple farms sell; too bad they don’t grow on trees,” DeLisle says. The income side of a New Hampshire orchard’s financial records is diverse and sometimes surprising; their expenses are just as interesting, he adds. The farmers are buying fuel, packaging, fertilizer,  and other supplies from local vendors, and are injecting yet more money into the local economy through the form of paychecks. “If we think about farms and the local economy, there are so many impacts that ripple through,” DeLisle says. Orchards are more economically generative than the typical farm because of agritourism, notes Gail McWilliam Jellie, agricultural program assistant for Extension. Pick-your-own operations are probably the original form of agritourism, McWilliam Jellie notes, but orchards go well beyond that, with lodging, weddings, field dinners, tractor- or horse-drawn wagon rides, petting farms, food trucks, and the list goes on. When people come to a New Hampshire orchard for one of these experiences, DeLisle says, they often come from out of state, and they are almost certainly going to engage with other local businesses while they’re here. And yet, even those approaches might not catch everything, adds Jesse Wright, another field specialist for Extension. She asserts that orchards and similar agricultural operations provide an economically significant benefit to the local environment and ecology through their land stewardship. “I think that is an important measure to include and will continue to increase in value as we see increasingly erratic weather patterns and stronger storms,” Wright says. 2026 is going to be a pivotal year for Tellman Hill, one in which the orchard will start welcoming guests to their own farm stand and their own orchard, fulfilling a dream they’ve each held for years. “It’s been great to have the support of UNH and folks that say, ‘Here’s what we can do for you,’ or, ‘What do you need?’” Morin says. title: Campus gun carry bill draws out student opinions on both sides - UnionLeader.com
content:

Travis Corcoran, R-Weare, will face a re… Despite a personal appeal from Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a pivotal … New Hampshire college students turned out both in support and against legislation that would allow students, staff and visitors to legally carry guns and other weapons on any public or private campus that receives government grants. University of New Hampshire Police Chief Steven Lee, inset, speaking at right, testified against legislation to allow anyone to carry weapons on any private or public college that receives government grants. State Rep. Samuel Farrington, R-Rochester, a University of New Hampshire senior, said campus policies restricting guns violate the U.S. Constitution and state law that gives the Legislature the sole authority to restrict access to firearms. “We in New Hampshire have made it crystal clear; self-defense is not a privilege, it is a natural right,” Farrington said Wednesday in presenting his bill (HB 1793). “No government, not a Legislature and certainly not a university bureaucrat, can take away that right.” Beni Griffin, a first-year UNH student, said the campus-carry bill would make the community much more insecure. “This does not increase safety; it increases the likelihood of accidental tragedy,” Griffin said. While Caleb Brower of Mont Vernon, a freshman history student at UNH, said he would have no interest in carrying a gun, he said, “I firmly believe allowing my colleagues to carry weapons on and off campus would further guarantee my own safety.” Both sides cited the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk on a college campus in September to buttress their case. Colin Patterson, a UNH freshman nursing student, said academic buildings are left open during the day, and that leaves students vulnerable. “It is possible that anyone can come in with a gun with bad intention,” said Patterson, who backs the bill. Rep. Timothy Horrigan, D-Durham, pointed out Utah had a similar law in place when Kirk was shot dead while speaking on a college campus. “Utah Valley University was not in fact a gun-free zone, but Kirk’s murderer was able to conceal his rifle on campus and was able to escape without any of the law-abiding citizens being able to return fire,” Horrigan noted. Steven Lee, UNH’s police chief, urged the House Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee to reject the bill and let colleges bar possession of weapons on campuses to maintain order. The campus police force is typically able to respond to an incident within 90 seconds, Lee said. At UNH, students and staff with guns must lock them up at the college police station. They can be taken out for someone to go to a firing range or to use the weapon to legally hunt game, Lee said. “Adding firearms, whether concealed or not, into a devolving dynamic situation is not helpful, not helpful to law enforcement or to the community at large,” Lee said. Dr. John Bunker, a UNH associate dean, said the bill could lead to more suicide incidents, as many students battle mental-health challenges. “College is often a pressure cooker,” Bunker said, adding a short time later, “The greatest threat of gun violence is the risk of self-harm, not an outside shooter.” Michael Glover, a UNH Ph.D. graduate, warned that adopting such a permissive law would prompt many students to leave New Hampshire colleges. “The best and brightest people will not come to this place if you play games like this,” Glover said. Michael Appleton, a Marine veteran and president of the student Senate at the NHTI, said bill opponents brand all students as too immature and weak to be responsible users of firearms. “I am shocked the attitude is that everyone is so suicidally incompetent that they aren’t able to defend their own rights,” Appleton said. What’s Next: The House panel is likely to recommend passage of this bill over the next two months. Outlook: Uncertain. Republican state senators have yet to sign onto the bill and Gov. Kelly Ayotte has yet to weigh in on it. title: Faculty Spotlight Jennifer Hammond, Ed.D. Alumna, Educator, and Lifelong Learner - University of New Hampshire
content: Jennifer Hammond brings a uniquely well-rounded perspective to her role as a faculty member at UNH College of Professional Studies Online. An alumna, current student, and educator, she has experienced UNH from nearly every angle including on campus, online, and as a working professional. With a career rooted in customer service, IT project management, and technical leadership, Jen is deeply committed to lifelong learning and to helping adult learners succeed by balancing technical expertise with human-centered leadership. How does being an alumna influence the way you teach and mentor students? I’m always going to be a student myself. My diverse academic and professional experiences help me understand different perspectives, challenges, and motivations. I’m currently still a student at UNH CPS Online, and I lead with curiosity and compassion in my teaching because that’s what I value most as a learner. What does the mission of UNH College of Professional Studies Online mean to you? Having been a residential student, a commuter, and an online learner, I truly understand the value of flexible education. Technology allows us to learn and teach from anywhere, and I’ve embraced the asynchronous online model to support adult learners who are balancing work, family, and other responsibilities. UNH CPS Online genuinely understands that adult learners have unique needs, and that’s reflected in its approach. I didn’t initially plan to work in technology, but the skills I gained became invaluable. I started in customer service and gradually moved into tech roles, wearing many hats—from application analyst to IT project manager. In my current role, I’ve developed skills in big data, which I find especially rewarding. Being a compassionate servant leader has always mattered to me, and combining that mindset with technical skills has opened doors I never expected. How can a technology-related degree prepare students for the future? IT is constantly changing and managing that change requires both technical knowledge and people skills. Today’s leaders need to understand the connection between technology and the humans who use it. A degree in technical management helps students develop this balance while building skills in project management, strategy, and governance, which are essential tools for leadership in the tech industry. What challenges should students be most prepared for? Emotional intelligence is more important than ever. IT managers need to stay current with technology, but they also need strong self-awareness, empathy, and communication skills. The field needs leaders who can balance technical expertise with genuine human connection. How do you bring real-world experience into the classroom? My career in technology has prepared me to bridge the gap between tech and people. I teach with a strong emphasis on trust, collaboration, and shared learning, encouraging students from different industries to learn from one another. I love being a small part of someone else’s success. I aim to create a safe, supportive learning environment where students can grow, build confidence, and expand their professional toolkits, all while continuing to learn alongside them. A luxury cruise ship that has been hit by an outbreak of the… The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it granted “expanded access” t… Dr. Thomas Fortney inside a patient room at New Hampshire Orthopaedic Center in Bedford, where a New Hampshire Union Leader story about his days playing hockey at the University of New Hampshire hangs on the wall. A framed New Hampshire Union Leader story from 2009 with the headline “One-two KO punch” hangs in the room where Dr. Thomas Fortney treats his patients. The news clipping serves as a lasting reminder of his time as a senior on the men’s hockey team at the University of New Hampshire when he netted the biggest goal that season: a dramatic game-tying score that came with just one-tenth of a second left on the clock. UNH ended up winning that game in overtime and advanced in the NCAA tournament to keep their season and Frozen Four hopes alive. “We went the furthest in the tournament that year. Unfortunately we didn’t win, but it was a good run for us,” he recalled. That stunning goal was a memorable one for Fortney, whose success on the ice in college has now carried over to his work as an orthopedic surgeon at New Hampshire Orthopaedic Center in Bedford, where he recently performed the first robotic-assisted total shoulder replacement in the state. The surgery, which was done at Elliot Hospital in Manchester, was also a milestone for the region as Connecticut was the only other New England state where such a procedure had been performed previously. Ties to UNH hockey run deep in this medical first. As it turns out, Ty Conklin, another former UNH hockey player, is a sales representative at Stryker, the medical technology company that developed the Mako robotic-assisted shoulder replacement system to improve accuracy. Conklin made a name for himself at UNH, earning several goaltending records. He went on to play professionally for teams in the NHL before retiring about 13 years ago. Fortney was approached by Stryker about performing this new surgery and was chosen following an interview process. He said robotic-assisted shoulder replacement is more precise than procedures performed manually. “All of the patients have been doing very well. Some of the patients have had both the standard shoulder replacement before and the robotic replacement on the other side and they’ve reported an even better and sometimes quick recovery so it does seem to have promising early results,” he said. Fortney discussed this new procedure during a public presentation in April at the Hotel Concord in Concord titled “Mako SmartRobotics: Robotic Surgery for Knee, Hip & Introducing Shoulder.” “After hip and knee replacement, this is the third most common joint replacement and in recent years it’s been the most rapidly growing in terms of the number of replacements of all of those replacements. Shoulder replacements have been performed for a long time, but we’ve seen a large uptick in recent years. I think newer technology has led to more success in those surgeries and therefore more people have learned about it and are willing to take that next step,” he said. Marc Richard, 65, of Loudon, is the patient who underwent the robotic-assisted procedure in December. He works in linen services at Elliot Hospital and had his right shoulder done last August and the robotic-assisted surgery on the left one. “I had a lot more movement in my left arm than I had with my right arm when he did it manually. It was unbelievable. He did a great job on my right shoulder, but the biggest difference between my right and my left was better movement and less pain. I’m also tracking twice as fast in (physical therapy) than I did with my right shoulder,” he said. If not for hockey, Fortney likely never would have become a player in New Hampshire’s medical community. He hails from St. Louis, Missouri, and came to New Hampshire to play for UNH when he was a freshman in 2005. “I had never been to New Hampshire before until I came to visit UNH. I fell in love with it there and had a great four years. We had a very good team at that time. We actually won the Hockey East’s regular season title two times, made it to the NCAA tournament all four years, which is a big accomplishment. We were very competitive,” he said. Fortney played semi-professional hockey in Germany for two years before deciding to begin pursuing a career in the medical field. A few years after graduation, he performed his orthopedic surgery residency at Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center, during which he served as the team doctor for the Dartmouth College football and men’s ice hockey teams. “My wife and I actually met while we were at Dartmouth. She’s a dermatologist and she was doing her residency at the same time. We both love this area. We love being close to the ocean and close to the mountains. We both have friends in the area and decided this was a great mutual place for us to settle,” he said. Fortney’s career path was inspired by his days on the ice in college and experience with his own sports-related injuries. Fortney, who specializes in shoulder, elbow and sports medicine, eventually decided to settle in Manchester and practice in New Hampshire about four years ago. He treats a number of athletes at the recreational, high school and college levels. While his college days are now behind him, Fortney is still in touch with some former classmates who live locally and work in the medical field. “It’s another connection we continue to have after college and after hockey,” he said. He and Conklin recently caught up at the Whittemore Center Arena for a photo shoot before the ice was removed for the season. “Being on the ice and looking up, it almost felt like my first time that I came to UNH. There was a feeling of excitement. Hard to believe that it was 20 years ago since I first arrived on campus. Sometimes it feels like just yesterday,” he said.
